input.question: A club has 12 members: 6 seniors, including Ana and Ben, and 6 juniors. A committee of exactly 5 members is chosen. It must contain at least 2 seniors, and Ana and Ben refuse to serve on the committee together (either one alone is fine). How many different committees are possible?

tier.name: medium

input.question: A data plan has a fixed monthly fee of $20. Usage is billed per whole gigabyte: the first 3 GB cost $4 per GB, the next 5 GB cost $8 per GB, and every GB after those costs $13 per GB. input.question:
A depot keeps a positive whole number of bottles in storage. The bottles are blue and the depot is open every day. The following facts are all true:

1. When it is counted in groups of 18, the last group is 11 short of a full group.
2. The number is exactly 13 more than a multiple of 30.
3. When it is counted in groups of 25, 8 bottles are left over.
4. When it is counted in groups of 21, the last group is 17 short of a full group.
5. The number is exactly 13 more than a multiple of 16.

What is the smallest possible number of bottles?
Answer format: a whole number.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Folded. Five remainder facts with moduli that share factors; merge them one at a time; about 12 minutes.

input.question:
On an island, every inhabitant is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Seven islanders meet: Zora, Xenia, Hana, Farid, Rafa, Brisa and Cato. Each of them makes exactly one statement:

Zora: "Cato and Hana are the same type."
Xenia: "At least one of Zora or Brisa is a knave."
Hana: "Farid and Zora are the same type."
Farid: "Xenia and Hana are of different types."
Rafa: "At least one of Hana or Brisa is a knave."
Brisa: "Among the seven of us, at least three are knaves."
Cato: "Among Zora, Hana and Rafa, at most one is a knave."

Exactly one assignment of knight or knave to the islanders fits all these statements. Find it.
Answer format: one word of 7 capital letters, one letter per islander in the order Zora, Xenia, Hana, Farid, Rafa, Brisa and Cato is listed above, K for a knight and N for a knave, with no spaces or other characters.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Folded. Seven islanders, seven statements, 128 cases cut by case analysis; about 20 minutes.

input.question:
A robot moves on a grid of intersections (x, y), where x is a whole number from 0 to 6 and y is a whole number from 0 to 6. It starts at (0, 0) and must reach (6, 6). Every move goes one step east (x increases by 1) or one step north (y increases by 1); it never moves west or south.

The intersections (0, 6), (2, 4), (3, 1), (5, 0) and (6, 5) are closed: the robot cannot enter them.
The path must pass through the intersection (3, 3).
The robot never makes more than three moves in the same direction in a row (so a run of four east moves, or four north moves, is not allowed).

Two paths are different if they visit different intersections or the same ones in a different order. How many different paths are possible?
Answer format: a whole number.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Folded. Paths on a 7 by 7 grid with five closed points, one required point and a cap on repeated moves; a table of about 50 cells by hand, about 25 minutes.

input.question:
Five people sit in a row of seats numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. Each person has a different first name (Farid, Jorun, Quill, Pavel and Hana), drinks a different drink (milk, water, soda, juice and coffee) and keeps a different pet (finch, goat, parrot, tortoise and falcon). Every name, drink and pet is used by exactly one person.

Clues:
1. Farid and the goat owner are the same person.
2. Exactly one seat lies between the water drinker and the parrot owner.
3. Farid sits somewhere to the left of Quill, not necessarily right next to Quill.
4. The soda drinker and the finch owner are the same person.
5. The falcon owner does not sit in seat 3.
6. The soda drinker sits somewhere to the left of Pavel, not necessarily right next to Pavel.
7. Exactly one seat lies between Pavel and Jorun.
8. The coffee drinker sits somewhere to the left of the goat owner, not necessarily right next to the goat owner.
9. The parrot owner sits somewhere to the left of Hana, not necessarily right next to Hana.
10. The juice drinker and the falcon owner are different people.

Which pet does the juice drinker keep?
Answer format: the one word naming that pet, spelled as in the text above.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Folded. Five seats, three traits and a dozen clues with a unique solution; a careful grid takes about 20 minutes.

input.question:

Job B: 5 hours; needs nothing.
Job C: 4 hours; needs E and H.

Job E: 4 hours; needs I.
Job F: 9 hours; needs I.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Folded. Nine jobs on two workers: build a schedule, then show that the next smaller finish is not possible; about 12 minutes.

Boxes: Small holds a total size of at most 10 and costs 7; Medium holds a total size of at most 17 and costs 11; Large holds a total size of at most 26 and costs 15. Any number of boxes of each type is available.

Rules:
1. Every parcel goes into exactly one box, and the sizes of the parcels in a box add up to at most the capacity of that box.
2. These pairs of parcels must not share a box: P1 and P11; P2 and P3; P4 and P10; P4 and P12; P4 and P13; P5 and P10; P7 and P12; P8 and P9; P9 and P13.

input.question:
A utility company must link 5 depots with underground cable. The 14 towns are Cawdor, Dunmore, Elwick, Fenham, Garth, Ingram, Kelby, Lorne, Marlow, Netley, Orsett, Penrith, Quenby, Ryhall. The depots are in Dunmore, Garth, Marlow, Netley, Orsett. Cable can be laid only along these routes, each with its price for the whole route:

Cawdor to Netley: 9; Cawdor to Ryhall: 10; Dunmore to Fenham: 3; Dunmore to Kelby: 4; Dunmore to Marlow: 10; Dunmore to Netley: 12; Dunmore to Ryhall: 8; Elwick to Lorne: 10; Elwick to Orsett: 8; Elwick to Penrith: 7; Garth to Orsett: 9; Garth to Penrith: 4; Garth to Quenby: 11; Garth to Ryhall: 12; Ingram to Kelby: 11; Ingram to Netley: 14; Ingram to Orsett: 4; Ingram to Quenby: 14; Ingram to Ryhall: 10; Kelby to Lorne: 8; Kelby to Marlow: 5; Kelby to Penrith: 13; Lorne to Marlow: 5; Lorne to Penrith: 12; Marlow to Orsett: 15; Netley to Ryhall: 6.

Rules:
1. The finished network must connect all depots: from any depot a person can walk to any other depot along laid cable. Cable may pass through any town, and a route is laid in full or not at all.
2. Every town that is not a depot charges a one-time junction fee if the network uses the town at all (that is, if any laid route starts or ends in it). Cable never passes through a town without a junction there. The fees are: Cawdor 4, Elwick 9, Fenham 4, Ingram 2, Kelby 7, Lorne 1, Penrith 3, Quenby 3, Ryhall 0. The depots charge no fee.
3. The cost of a network is the sum of the prices of the routes laid plus the junction fees of the towns it uses.

What is the smallest possible total cost?

shortcuts.name: join the nearest unconnected depot, starting from the first depot
the same from every depot, then the cheapest network on the towns used
shortest routes between depots, join the two nearest first, then the cheapest network on the towns used
cheapest cable network over all towns, then cut every dead end that is not a depot

tier.name: extra-hard
tier.basis: Estimate, not timed: 14 towns, 5 depots, 26 routes and junction fees; build networks with the usual constructions, then check by dynamic programming over groups of depots (or by trying sets of junction towns) that none is cheaper.

3. The first job needs no setup. The machine is idle only when it waits for a release or a setup.
4. The cost of a plan is the sum, over all jobs, of (weight x finish time).

The setup times s(X,Y), with the job just finished in the row and the next job in the column:

from \ to     A  B  C  D  E  F  G  H  I

Rules for a legal plan:

Each district needs a number of masts that cover it: D1 needs 1; D2 needs 1; D3 needs 2; D4 needs 1; D5 needs 1; D6 needs 1; D7 needs 1; D8 needs 2; D9 needs 1; D10 needs 2; D11 needs 2; D12 needs 1; D13 needs 2; D14 needs 1. input.question:
Turn the word "tpnkptmeenukddmkdk" (18 letters) into the word "tpnkppeakattmeenukrdmka" (23 letters) with the cheapest set of edits. Every edit works on one letter:

1. A letter of the first word may be kept (cost 0), if it is placed against the same letter of the second word.
2. A letter of the first word may be replaced by a letter of the second word. The cost is 1 when the two letters are in the same class and 3 when they are in different classes.
   The classes are: a e o u | d t k p | m n r l.
3. Letters of the first word that are left over may be deleted, and letters of the second word that are left over may be inserted. Look at the stretch between two neighbouring placed pairs of letters (kept or replaced), or before the first pair, or after the last pair. The k letters of the first word that are deleted in that stretch form one run and cost 4 + k together. The k letters of the second word that are inserted in that stretch form another run and cost 4 + k together. A stretch has at most one deletion run and at most one insertion run, and the two runs are paid separately.
4. Letters keep their order: if one letter of the first word is placed against a letter of the second word, every letter before it is placed against letters before it.

What is the smallest possible total cost?
Answer format: a whole number, with no units.

shortcuts.name: fewest edits (every edit costs 1), priced with the real costs
every replacement 3 and every gap letter 3 (no run discount), priced with the real costs
always take the cheapest next step
keep a longest common subsequence, pair and gap the rest
pair the letters in order, then one gap for the length difference

tier.name: extra-hard
tier.basis: Estimate, not timed: two words of about 20 letters; a three-table dynamic programme (match, deletion run, insertion run) of about 400 cells filled by hand with care, plus a check of a few alternative alignments.
